Что касается до величайшаго пременения которое производит и произвесть может
сие возсоединение огня со светомъ въ скотскомъ естестве человека, прежде нежели совершенно
разрушится оно временною смертию, то пременение сее вторично преобразовано павли=
номъ. Хвостъ его теперь уже совсемъ сложенъ и опущенъ до самой земли; глаза его
непрестанно устремлены на черныя безобразныя ноги и переднюю его часть, озаряе=
мую некоторыми лучами великаго небеснаго солнца: ибо разумная и чувственная
часть человека ни какъ неможетъ узреть въ самой подлинности мрачнаго, немощ=
наго, суетнаго и злаго основания на которомъ она стоитъ, естьли не коснутся ея
некоторые лучи преестественнаго солнца.— Две вещи надлежитъ заметить
еще въ разсуждении сего павлина: 1е Павлинь сей, которой въ прежнемъ изображении
означенъ былъ на цѣломъ стане или тѣлѣ человѣка, какъ существенная часть
его самаго находится теперь нъ особливой отдѣленной половинѣ стана и можетъ
самъ по себѣ удобно снятъ быть и отнятъ отъ человѣка. Сие показываетъ, что
по возсоединении скотское естество: а тѣмъ болѣе весь нарочный видимый чело=
вѣкъ: хотя и пребываетъ еще въ собственной своей сферѣ; однако не столь уже
тѣсно, не столь внутренно, не столь подлинно и не столь обыкновенно соединенъ
съ человѣкомъ а соединенъ съ нимъ подной только внѣшности. 2е Павлинь
сей въ прежнемъ изображении представленъ былъ съ натворениемъ внутри те=
мнѣйшей окружности мрачнаго міра, которой находился на той же повер=
ности противъ составившей окружности свѣтлаго міра, но теперь оная
мрачная окружность совершенно изчезла изъ глазъ и не видна уже въ настоя=
щемъ изображении, а видна токмо свѣтлѣйшая окружность свѣтлаго міра,

Regarding the greatest transformation that this reunification of fire with light can produce and has produced in the <term>animal nature</term> <gloss>the base, instinctual part of human nature</gloss> of man, before it is completely destroyed by temporal death, this transformation is represented a second time by a peacock. Its tail is now completely folded and lowered to the very ground. Its eyes are constantly fixed upon its black, unsightly feet and its front part, which is illuminated by certain rays of the great heavenly sun. For the rational and sensory part of man can in no way behold, in its true reality, the dark, weak, vain, and evil foundation upon which it stands, unless it is touched by some rays of the supernatural sun. Two things should still be noted regarding this peacock:

1. This peacock, which in the previous illustration was marked upon the whole frame or body of man as an essential part of himself, is now found in a special, separate half of the frame. It can easily be removed and taken away from the person by itself. This shows that after the reunification, the animal nature—and even more so the entire intentional, visible man—although still remaining in its own sphere, is no longer so closely, so inwardly, so truly, and so commonly united with the man. Instead, it is united with him only in external appearance.

2. This peacock in the previous illustration was presented with an intent within the darkest circumference of the dark world, which was located on the same surface opposite the circumference that formed the light world. But now that dark circumference has completely vanished from sight and is no longer visible in the present illustration. Only the brightest circumference of the light world is visible,

They knew him from afar as he drew near,—gathered around him,—and then assailed him with taunts from this side and from that, every man of them,—calling him 'that kinsman of the maniac, of the plotter against the host,'—saying that he should not save himself from being mangled to death by stoning. And so they had come to this, that swords plucked from sheaths were drawn in men's hands; then the strife, when it had run well-nigh to the furthest, was allayed by the soothing words of elders. But where shall I find Ajax, to tell him this? He whom most it touches must hear all the tale.

CH. He is not within; he hath gone forth but now; for he hath yoked a new purpose to his new mood.

**730** *κολεῶν*] *κουλεῶν* r.—*διεπεραιώθη*] The scribe of L wrote *διεπαιρεώθη* (transposing ε and αι): S has corrected ε to αι, but the αι after π has been allowed to remain: a later hand has placed dots over it. **733** *πού στιν* L, with the mark of aphaeresis (') just over π, not in front of σ: a curious error, suggestive of mechanical copying. **735 f.** Nauck, objecting to *ἐγκαταζεύξας*, would write, *οὐκ ἔνδον ἀνήρ, ἀλλὰ φροῦδος ἀρτίως, | βουλὰς νέας νέοισιν ἁρμόσας τρόποις.*

---

dying: schol. *ὡς οὐκ ἀρκέσοι ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ λιθόλευστος γενέσθαι.* Cp. Aesch. *P. V.* 918 *οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ ταῦτ' ἐπαρκέσει τὸ μὴ οὐ | πεσεῖν ἀτίμως.* For the fut. optat., cp. 313.—**καταξανθείς**, carded (like wool), torn to shreds; Eur. imitates this (*Suppl.* 503) *πέτροις καταξανθέντες ὀστέων ῥαφάς.* Cp. Ar. *Ach.* 319 *τί φειδόμεσθα τῶν λίθων, ὦ δημόται, | μὴ οὐ καταξαίνειν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον εἰς φοινικίδα;*

**729 f.** **ὥστ'** ('and so') has been suspected on account of the second **ὥστε**: but the latter, going with **τοσοῦτον**, does not offend the ear, since its sense is different and subordinate; cp. *Ant.* 735 *ὁρᾷς τόδ' ὡς εἴρηκας ὡς ἄγαν νέος*; *Tr.* 1241 *τάχ', ὡς ἔοικας, ὡς νοσεῖς φράσεις.* So in Xen. *Anab.* 2. 2. 17 *κραυγὴν.. ἐποίουν,.. ὥστε καὶ τοὺς πολεμίους ἀκούειν· ὥστε οἱ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω.. ἔφυγον*: where the first *ὥστε* = 'so that,' while the second = 'and so.'

**κολεῶν.. ξίφη.** The swords **διεπεραιώθη** *κολεῶν*, were drawn through (and out of) the scabbards, **ἐρυστά**, by a sharp, quick pull,—*i.e.* with angry haste.—Not, 'swords plucked from the sheaths were *crossed*': as if Teucer actually crossed swords with one or more of his assailants. The whole scene has been suggested by that in the first book of the *Iliad*, as the schol. in L saw:—*ἐκ τῆς Ἀχιλλέως δὲ πρὸς Ἀγαμέμνονα ἀρχῆς* (read *ὀργῆς*) *παραγέγραπται.* There, Achilles was drawing his sword—*ἕλκετο δ' ἐκ κολεοῖο μέγα ξίφος*—when Athena came to him

<column-break/>

(*Il.* 1. 194): *ἂψ δ' ἐς κουλεὸν ὦσε μέγα ξίφος* (*ib.* 220).—Some of the later MSS. here have **κουλεῶν**, which was a current form in late Greek (Eustathius p. 1604. 58 *τὸ κολεὸν κοινότερον κουλεὸν λέγεται*).

**731 f.** **δραμοῦσα τοῦ προσωτάτω**: for the partitive gen., cp. Xen. *Anab.* 1. 3. 1 *οὐκ ἔφασαν ἰέναι τοῦ πρόσω*: Ar. *Ran.* 174 *ὑπάγεθ' ὑμεῖς τῆς ὁδοῦ.*—**ἐν ξυναλλαγῇ λόγου.. γερόντων**, by means of the conciliatory words of elders: for the double gen., cp. 308 f.: for **ἐν**, denoting the instrument, *Ph.* 60 *ἐν λιταῖς στείλαντες*, *ib.* 1393 *ἐν λόγοις | πείσειν.*

**733 f.** **ἡμὶν**, ethic dat.: *O. C.* 81 *ἦ βέβηκεν ἡμὶν ὁ ξένος;*—**τοῖς κυρίοις**, *i.e.*, Ajax himself, who is the *κύριος* or 'principal person' in this matter, as being most nearly concerned in it. For the poet. plur., cp. Aesch. *Ch.* 688 (Orestes to Clytaemnestra) *εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω | τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων | οὐκ οἶδα.*

**735 f.** **νέας βουλάς**, his new 'counsels,' in respect of his supposed resolve to propitiate gods and men; **νέοισιν.. τρόποις**, the new 'dispositions,' the character of greater gentleness and docility, which the resolve implies. **ἐγκαταζεύξας**: he has 'harnessed' the new resolve, as it were, to the new character,—brought it under the yoke of his chastened will. The word conveys more than the idea of 'adapting' (Pindar's *ἔργμασιν νικαφόροις ἐγκώμιον ζεῦξαι μέλος*, *N.* 1. 7). It further implies self-conquest.

<meta>Page number 115; running header "AJAX"; signature 8—2. This page holds the English translation of lines 727 to 736, the textual notes, and the commentary. The commentary continues the note from the previous page on "saying he would not be able to save himself from... dying."</meta>

They knew him from afar as he drew near, gathered around him, and then assailed him with taunts from this side and from that, every man of them, calling him 'that kinsman of the maniac, of the plotter against the host,' saying that he should not save himself from being mangled to death by stoning. And so they had come to this, that swords plucked from sheaths were drawn in men's hands; then the strife, when it had run well-nigh to the furthest, was allayed by the soothing words of elders. But where shall I find Ajax, to tell him this? He whom most it touches must hear all the tale.

CHORUS. He is not within; he hath gone forth but now; for he hath yoked a new purpose to his new mood.

**730** *<term>koleōn</term>* <gloss>from the sheaths</gloss>: some later manuscripts read *<term>kouleōn</term>*.—*<term>dieperaiōthē</term>* <gloss>were drawn through</gloss>: The scribe of L <note>the Laurentian manuscript in Florence, the oldest and most important manuscript of Sophocles</note> wrote *<term>diepaireōthē</term>* (transposing e and ai). S <note>a corrector of L</note> has corrected e to ai, but the ai after p has been allowed to remain; a later hand has placed dots over it. **733** *<term>pou stin</term>* <gloss>where is he?</gloss> in L, with the mark of <term>aphaeresis</term> <gloss>the dropping of an initial vowel</gloss> (') placed just over the p, not in front of the s: a curious error, suggestive of mechanical copying. **735 f.** Nauck, objecting to *<term>enkatazeuxas</term>* <gloss>having yoked</gloss>, would write: "The man is not within, but gone just now, having fitted new counsels to new ways." <note>original: "οὐκ ἔνδον ἀνήρ, ἀλλὰ φροῦδος ἀρτίως, | βουλὰς νέας νέοισιν ἁρμόσας τρόποις."</note>

---

dying: the scholiast explains, "that it would not avail him to escape being stoned." <note>original: "ὡς οὐκ ἀρκέσοι ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ λιθόλευστος γενέσθαι."</note> Compare Aeschylus, *Prometheus Bound* 918: "for these things will in no way suffice to save him from falling dishonourably." <note>original: "οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ ταῦτ' ἐπαρκέσει τὸ μὴ οὐ | πεσεῖν ἀτίμως."</note> For the future optative, compare line 313.—**<term>kataxantheis</term>** <gloss>carded</gloss>, carded like wool, that is, torn to shreds. Euripides imitates this (*Suppliants* 503): "carded by stones in the seams of their bones." <note>original: "πέτροις καταξανθέντες ὀστέων ῥαφάς."</note> Compare Aristophanes, *Acharnians* 319: "Why do we spare our stones, fellow demesmen, instead of carding this fellow into a scarlet rag?" <note>original: "τί φειδόμεσθα τῶν λίθων, ὦ δημόται, | μὴ οὐ καταξαίνειν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον εἰς φοινικίδα;" The "scarlet rag" puns on the red cloak of Athenian soldiers.</note>

**729 f.** **<term>hōst'</term>** <gloss>and so</gloss> has been suspected on account of the second **<term>hōste</term>**. But the latter, going with **<term>tosouton</term>** <gloss>so far</gloss>, does not offend the ear, since its sense is different and subordinate. Compare *Antigone* 735: "Do you see how you have spoken this, like one far too young?" <note>original: "ὁρᾷς τόδ' ὡς εἴρηκας ὡς ἄγαν νέος"</note>; *Trachiniae* 1241: "Soon, it seems, you will show how sick you are." <note>original: "τάχ', ὡς ἔοικας, ὡς νοσεῖς φράσεις."</note> So also in Xenophon, *Anabasis* 2. 2. 17: "they raised a shout... so that even the enemy heard it; and so those nearest... fled." <note>original: "κραυγὴν.. ἐποίουν,.. ὥστε καὶ τοὺς πολεμίους ἀκούειν· ὥστε οἱ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω.. ἔφυγον"</note> Here the first *hōste* means 'so that,' while the second means 'and so.'

**<term>koleōn.. xiphē</term>** <gloss>swords... from the sheaths</gloss>. The swords **<term>dieperaiōthē</term>** *<term>koleōn</term>*, were drawn through and out of the scabbards, **<term>erusta</term>** <gloss>plucked</gloss>, by a sharp, quick pull, that is, with angry haste. The meaning is not 'swords plucked from the sheaths were *crossed*,' as if Teucer actually crossed swords with one or more of his assailants. The whole scene has been suggested by the one in the first book of the *Iliad*, as the scholiast in L saw: "it has been modelled on the anger of Achilles against Agamemnon" <note>original: "ἐκ τῆς Ἀχιλλέως δὲ πρὸς Ἀγαμέμνονα ἀρχῆς"; the manuscript reads <term>archēs</term> <gloss>beginning</gloss>, which Jebb corrects to <term>orgēs</term> <gloss>anger</gloss>.</note>. There, Achilles was drawing his sword, "and he was drawing his great sword from its sheath" <note>original: "ἕλκετο δ' ἐκ κολεοῖο μέγα ξίφος"</note>, when Athena came to him

<column-break/>

(*Iliad* 1. 194): "and back into the sheath he thrust the great sword" <note>original: "ἂψ δ' ἐς κουλεὸν ὦσε μέγα ξίφος"</note> (same book, line 220).—Some of the later manuscripts here have **<term>kouleōn</term>**, which was a current form in late Greek. Eustathius, p. 1604. 58, says: "the sheath, <term>koleon</term>, is more commonly called <term>kouleon</term>." <note>original: "τὸ κολεὸν κοινότερον κουλεὸν λέγεται." Eustathius was a 12th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator on Homer.</note>

**731 f.** **<term>dramousa tou prosōtatō</term>** <gloss>having run to the furthest point</gloss>: for the partitive genitive, compare Xenophon, *Anabasis* 1. 3. 1: "they said they would not go further" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔφασαν ἰέναι τοῦ πρόσω"</note>; Aristophanes, *Frogs* 174: "move along on your way" <note>original: "ὑπάγεθ' ὑμεῖς τῆς ὁδοῦ."</note>—**<term>en xunallagē logou.. gerontōn</term>** <gloss>by the reconciling speech of elders</gloss>, that is, by means of the conciliatory words of the elders. For the double genitive, compare lines 308 f. For **<term>en</term>** <gloss>in, by</gloss> denoting the instrument, compare *Philoctetes* 60: "having sent with entreaties" <note>original: "ἐν λιταῖς στείλαντες"</note>, and the same play, 1393: "to persuade by words" <note>original: "ἐν λόγοις | πείσειν."</note>

**733 f.** **<term>hēmin</term>** <gloss>for us</gloss>, an ethic dative, expressing the speaker's interest. Compare *Oedipus at Colonus* 81: "Has the stranger gone from us?" <note>original: "ἦ βέβηκεν ἡμὶν ὁ ξένος;"</note>—**<term>tois kuriois</term>** <gloss>to those with authority</gloss>, that is, Ajax himself, who is the *<term>kurios</term>* <gloss>principal person</gloss> in this matter, as the one most nearly concerned in it. For the poetic plural, compare Aeschylus, *Libation Bearers* 688, where Orestes says to Clytemnestra: "but whether I happen to be speaking to those with authority and concern in the matter, I do not know." <note>original: "εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω | τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων | οὐκ οἶδα."</note>

**735 f.** **<term>neas boulas</term>** <gloss>new counsels</gloss>: his new 'counsels,' in respect of his supposed resolve to propitiate gods and men. **<term>neoisin.. tropois</term>** <gloss>to new ways</gloss>: the new 'dispositions,' the character of greater gentleness and docility which that resolve implies. **<term>enkatazeuxas</term>** <gloss>having yoked</gloss>: he has 'harnessed' the new resolve, as it were, to the new character, bringing it under the yoke of his chastened will. The word conveys more than the idea of 'adapting,' as in Pindar's "to yoke a song of praise to victorious deeds" <note>original: "ἔργμασιν νικαφόροις ἐγκώμιον ζεῦξαι μέλος"</note> (*Nemean Odes* 1. 7). It further implies self-conquest.

<summary>Jebb's English rendering of Ajax lines 727 to 736 describes how the Greek army threatened Teucer with stoning and drawn swords until the elders calmed them, and the Chorus reports that Ajax has gone out with a "new purpose." The textual notes and commentary discuss manuscript errors in L, the Homeric model for the sword-drawing scene, and grammatical points such as the partitive genitive, the ethic dative, and the force of the verb "yoked."</summary>
<keywords>Sophocles, Ajax, Teucer, Achilles, Agamemnon, Athena, Jebb commentary, stoning, scabbard, sword, Iliad book 1, Laurentian manuscript, scholia, Nauck, Eustathius, aphaeresis, partitive genitive, ethic dative, double genitive, textual criticism, Aeschylus, Euripides Suppliants, Aristophanes Acharnians, Xenophon Anabasis, Pindar, self-conquest</keywords>

ἀμφοτέρω δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς τὸν Πόντον τιμῆς, τὸν μὲν αὐτὴν τὴν Θρᾴκιον βόσπορον· ὁ
δὲ ὀνομαζόμενος ἴδιος, λέγεται δὲ βόσπορος τὴν φυγάδα τὴν πρὸς τὸν Πόντον αὐτὴν
δὲ καὶ τὰ πρὸς τὸν αἰγιαλὸν Ἑλλήσποντον· μεῖζον τὸ χάσμα, ταῖς αἰγιαλαῖς πηγαῖς·
ὁ δὲ δὲ ὅτι καὶ καλῶς πεπόρευται ὁ Διονύσιος ἀμφοτέρω τῷ πορθμῷ.

The memory says that a bronze cow stood at this passage, having been set up by the Chalcedonians; for both this and those were the monument of the beautiful heifer. And this bull was called Thracian from the Thracian living around the place. Just as it was once called by the same name as this greater one. Dionysius <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer</note> says about this that its narrowest part ferries that whole thing, and those who have become sea-faring through the wave-swept [strait]; these are the prodigies who reveal such a Byzantine strait, and the historians use "heifer." But this geographer is accustomed to calling the Byzantine strait the "Thracian cow." And the prodigies call the Hellespont strait [the cow] over all the parents before the Thracian one came to be, and the geographer likewise records those on the stages in the strait, interpreting it. It must be noted that this, and all the local differences, the Thracian cow is what pours out toward the Pontus; the northern part is its own, the southern is that of the Propontis. And they know that the mouth of the Pontus will appear more accurately as the Hellespont of the Chalcedonians; for it is very close to the beginning of Dionysius, the waves and by Cyzicus, just as he himself says, and others not toward the whole place. But his scope of the Hellespont and that passage toward the Pontus is the remainder; therefore, let us also go to the widths themselves. Its northern [part] and the northern one toward the Pontus, that which is after the Hellespont; and after the Pontus, that which is toward the north is the mouth of the Pontus. These things have ambiguities because the ancients called the parts by Abydos the Hellespont, and the Pontus the Hellespont; others also [called] the whole Pontus. And the northern one is that toward the mouth of the Pontus; regarding this, those around Heracles despaired of the Hellespont. Others [call] the Aegean source of the Hellespont toward the north, as perhaps Homer does; the ocean toward the widths and the Hellespont. And I seem to follow Dionysius in these things, as it is necessary to divide [them] and [as] water of an exit; so that the Hellespont is the narrow channel, and the Pontus. And both are from the honor toward the Pontus, the one being the Thracian Bosphorus itself. And the one called personal, the Bosphorus is said to be the fugitive toward the Pontus itself, and the parts toward the shore the Hellespont; the chasm is greater, with the shore sources. And [it is] because Dionysius has also traveled well through both straits.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is perfected. The capacity for complete enjoyment is the <term>Sambhogakāya</term> <gloss>complete enjoyment body</gloss>. Alternatively, the body that is experienced is the complete enjoyment body. Or, the body existing for the sake of complete enjoyment is the complete enjoyment body. Its nature is the perfection of one's own welfare while accomplishing the welfare of others, radiant with the major marks and minor signs. Alternatively, that which fully sustains the bodhisattvas by teaching the profound and vast Dharma, or genuinely pleases them, is the complete enjoyment body. Or, that which operates everywhere through the bodhisattvas experiencing the expressed meanings taught in those doctrines is the complete enjoyment body.

The emanation is emanation itself; the body established by that is the <term>Nirmāṇakāya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. Furthermore, accomplishing completely and without exception all higher states and definitive goodness everywhere, throughout all time, as long as cyclic existence lasts, as long as space endures, according to appropriate times and dispositions, constitutes the activity of emanation and the emanation body. Its essence consists of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and others, the perfection of the welfare of self and others.

Likewise, the great lay practitioner <term>Candragomin</term> <gloss>Moon Layman</gloss> declared regarding the <term>Dharmakāya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss>:

The truth body of this is suchness,
Not an object within the domain of conceptual thoughts.
The nature of sentient beings and reality
Are non-dual with respect to that.

The bodies of various essences,
And the essential natures of wandering beings,
Become of a single flavor in it,
Like rivers flowing into the ocean.

Such a body as this
Is the truth body of the Protectors.
Completely purified in all aspects,
It is the very domain of perfect awakening.

Through its innate power,
Accomplishing boundless benefit in the world
At all times
Is like the rays of the sun.

Regarding the complete enjoyment body:

Relinquishing the self like one born blind,
Those who have accumulated merit themselves
See it alone and all at once,
Just like the sun seen by all.

Relinquishing the self like the deaf,
With ears enriched by the wealth of merit,
The elixir of the sublime Dharma's nectar
Unto that, that

<summary>This passage provides definitions and functions of the three bodies of the Buddha: the complete enjoyment body, the emanation body, and the truth body. It cites verses by the Indian master Candragomin illustrating how the truth body unifies all beings and how purified disciples perceive the complete enjoyment body.</summary>

# Gründliche Erklärung

Erkäntniß des HErrn werden erfüllet seyn; so ist doch nicht ein jeder unter denen/ die von Anbeginn sind Philister/ Tyrer und Mohren gewesen/ zu Zion gebohren. Darum muß solches in denen Ewigkeiten geschehen. Daß aber ein jeglicher unter denen/ die ehemals Philister/ Tyrer und Mohren gewesen sind/ zu Zion müsse gebohren werden/ erhellet aus der Grund-Sprache gantz deutlich. Denn in derselbigen heißt die Redens-Art/ Philistea dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ so viel/ als ein jeglicher unter allen/ die in Philistea gewohnet haben/ ist daselbst gebohren/ also heißt/ Tyrus dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ so viel/ als ein jeder unter allen/ die zu Tyro ehemals gewohnet haben/ ist daselbst gebohren. Und die Redens-Art/ die Mohren dieser ist daselbst gebohren/ heißt so viel/ als ein jeder unter allen Mohren/ die ehemals auf dem Erdboden gewesen sind/ hat sich zu GOtt gekehret/ und ist ein Heiliger worden. Mohren aber werden in der heiligen Schrifft nicht nur die genennet/ welche eine schwarze Haut haben/ sondern auch die/ welche ein schwarzes Herz haben/ das ist/ alle Kinder der Finsterniß. Dessen finden wir ein Exempel in dem siebenden Psalm/ allwo vers 1. von dem Simei/ der ein gebohrner Israelite/ aus dem Stamm Benjamin war/ um seiner schwarzen Sitten und Untugend willen gesagt wird/ er sey ein Mohr. Eben also sind alle Menschen/ die in der Finsterniß wandeln/ und Böses thun/ nichts anders denn Mohren. Diese Mohren haben zwar eine geraume Zeit einen rechten Greuel an Zion; es wird aber noch dahin kommen/ daß ein jeder unter ihnen seine alte Adamische Mohren-Geburt wird müssen verfluchen/ und von neuem aus Zion gebohren werden. Denn der HErr hat es gesagt.

Vers 5.

Und zu Zion wird gesaget werden/ ein Mann und Mann ist in ihr gebohren: Ein Mann und Mann/ heißt nach der Hebräischen Redens-Art so viel/ als ein jeglicher/ Niemand ausgenommen. So soll dann ein jeder Mensch/ er mag seyn wer er will/ und mag gelebet haben zu welcher Zeit/ und an welchem Ort er will/ noch endlich in Zion gebohren werden. Selig ist der und heilig/ welcher bald/ da er noch im Leibe lebet/ sich aus GOtt wiedergebären und erneuern läßt. Der wird mit Christo/ für GOtt/ in die Ewigkeiten derer Ewigkeiten/ ein Priester seyn. Wer aber zärtlich ist/ und die geistlichen Geburts-Schmerzen nicht ausstehen/ sondern nach dem Fleisch leben will/ der verscherzet das Recht der Erstgeburt/ und kan dennoch/ nach ausgestandener grosser Quaal/ an dem Leibe und an der Seelen/ denen geistlichen Geburts-Schmerzen nicht entgehen/ wie geschrieben stehet: Die

<column-break/>

Geburts-Schmerzen einer Gebärerin sollen ihm kommen: Er ist ein Sohn/ der nicht weise ist/ denn er stehet nicht die rechte Zeit in der Bär-Mutter der Kinder/ Hos. 13/13. Diß ist so viel gesaget/ als/ wer in dieser Welt/ die rechte Zeit/ in der geistlichen Bär-Mutter GOttes/ in welcher er zu einem ganz neuen und heiligen Leben soll wiedergebohren werden/ nicht ausstehen kan/ der soll die Geburts-Schmerzen/ vor welchen ihm in dieser Welt gegrauet hat/ in der Hölle fühlen. Von dieser geistlichen Bär-Mutter redet GOtt/ durch seinen Knecht Jesaiam/ wenn er spricht: Höret mir zu/ ihr vom Hause Jacob/ und alle übrigen/ vom Hause Israel/ die ihr von mir im Leibe getragen werdet/ und mir in der Mutter liegt/ Jes. 46/1. Gleichwie ein leibliches Kind/ das nicht seine rechte Zeit in der Mutter bleibet/ sondern ehe/ denn es zeitig ist/ abgehet/ eine unzeitige Geburt ist/ und nicht leben kan; eben also verhält sichs auch im Geistlichen. Wer GOtt dem HErrn nicht in der Mutter liegen bleibet/ biß daß er alle Glieder des neuen Menschen in gehöriger Vollkommenheit erlanget hat/ also daß er tüchtig ist/ für GOtt im Geiste zu wandeln/ der hat kein Theil an dem herrlichen Reiche JEsu Christi/ sondern muß so lange in der Hölle liegen/ biß er/ nach gnugsam ausgestandenen Geburts-Schmerzen/ wieder daraus erlöset wird. Wie dann GOtt spricht: ich will sie erlösen aus der Hölle/ und vom Tode erretten. Tod/ ich will dir ein Gifft seyn/ Hölle/ ich will dir eine Pestilenz seyn. Hos. 13/14. Daß in diesen Worten von keiner verblümten/ sondern von der recht eigentlichen Hölle gehandelt werde/ ist aus denen vorhergehenden Versen offenbar. Denn im siebenden und achten Vers sprach GOtt: So will ich auch werden gegen sie/ wie ein Löwe/ und wie ein Pardel auf dem Wege will ich auf sie lauren. Ich will ihnen begegnen wie ein Bär/ dem seine Jungen genommen sind/ und will ihr verstocktes Herz zerreissen/ und will sie daselbst wie ein Löwe fressen/ die wilden Thier sollen sie zerreissen. Und im zwölfften Vers heißt es: Die Missethat Ephraim ist zusammen gebunden/ und ihre Sünde ist behalten. Wer siehet hier nicht/ daß alle dieselbigen/ welche GOtt gefressen hat wie ein Löwe/ und denen die Sünde behalten ist/ in der recht eigentlich also genannten Hölle sind. Und dennoch heißt es: ich will sie erlösen aus der Hölle. Darum bleibet es dabey/ ein Mann und Mann/ das ist/ ein jeder Mensch/ muß in Zion gebohren werden. Diese göttliche Wahrheit gehöret unter keinen Scheffel/ und ist GOttes Wille durchaus nicht/ daß man sie verschweigen soll/ wie es dann heißt: Zu Zion wird gesaget werden.

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: the lake of fire. This is</meta> the second death. Then after that, death and hell are no more. Since the knowledge of the Lord shall be filled, yet not every one among those who from the beginning were Philistines, Tyrians, and Moors was born to Zion. Therefore, such must happen in the ages <note>original: "in denen Ewigkeiten," referring to the successive eons of time</note>. That every single person among those who were formerly Philistines, Tyrians, and Moors must be born to Zion is clearly evident from the original language. For in that language, the manner of speaking—"Philistia, this one was born there"—means as much as: every single one among all who lived in Philistia was born there. Likewise, "Tyre, this one was born there" means every one among all who formerly lived in Tyre was born there. And the expression "the Moors, this one was born there" <note>Referring to Psalm 87:4. The term "Moors" here refers to Ethiopians or those from the land of Cush</note> means as much as: every one among all Moors who were formerly on the face of the earth has turned to God and become a saint. In Holy Scripture, however, not only those who have black skin are called <term>Mohren</term> <gloss>Moors</gloss>, but also those who have a black heart; that is, all children of darkness. We find an example of this in the seventh Psalm, where in verse 1 it is said of Shimei—who was a natural-born Israelite from the tribe of Benjamin—that he was a <term>Mohr</term> <gloss>Moor</gloss> because of his black character and vice. In the same way, all people who walk in darkness and do evil are nothing other than Moors. These Moors, indeed, for a long time hold Zion in true abomination; but it will yet come to the point that every one among them must curse his old Adamite Moorish birth and be born anew out of Zion. For the Lord has spoken it.

### Verse 5.

And of Zion it shall be said, a man and a man is born in her. "A man and a man" <note>original: "ein Mann und Mann"</note> means, according to the Hebrew idiom, as much as: every single one, none excepted. Thus, every human being, whoever he may be and in whatever time or place he may have lived, shall finally be born in Zion. Blessed and holy is he who soon, while he still lives in the body, allows himself to be reborn and renewed by God. He shall be a priest with Christ, before God, into the ages of ages. But he who is delicate and cannot endure the spiritual birth pains, but wishes to live according to the flesh, forfeits the right of the firstborn. Yet even he, after enduring great torment in body and soul, cannot escape the spiritual birth pains, as it is written: The

<column-break/>

birth pains of a woman in travail shall come upon him: he is an unwise son, for he does not stand at the right time in the <term>Bär-Mutter</term> <gloss>womb or motherly source</gloss> of children <note>Hosea 13:13</note>. This is as much as to say: whoever in this world cannot endure the right time in the spiritual womb of God—in which he is to be reborn to a completely new and holy life—shall feel the birth pains in hell, the very ones he dreaded in this world. God speaks of this spiritual womb through his servant Isaiah when he says: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb <note>Isaiah 46:1</note>. Just as a physical child who does not remain his proper time in the mother, but passes away before it is ripe, is an untimely birth and cannot live; so it is also in spiritual matters. Whoever does not remain lying in the mother for the Lord God until he has attained all the members of the new man in proper perfection—so that he is fit to walk in the spirit before God—has no part in the glorious kingdom of Jesus Christ, but must lie in hell so long until he is released from it again after sufficiently enduring birth pains. As God then says: I will ransom them from the power of hell and redeem them from death. O death, I will be thy plague; O hell, I will be thy destruction <note>Hosea 13:14</note>. That these words deal not with a figurative but with the actual, literal hell is obvious from the preceding verses. For in the seventh and eighth verses God spoke: Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I observe them. I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lion: the wild beast shall tear them. And in the twelfth verse it says: The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hid. Who does not see here that all those whom God has devoured like a lion, and whose sin is retained, are in the place properly called hell. And yet it says: I will ransom them from hell. Therefore it stands: a man and a man—that is, every single human being—must be born in Zion. This divine truth belongs under no bushel, and it is by no means God's will that one should keep silent about it, as it is said: Of Zion it shall be said.
